title: 04 — Camera and capture filename patterns (P5's `filename_pattern`)
owner: P5 (injected) — the observation it produces is consumed by P6
consumer: the caller-supplied `filename_pattern(filename) -> str | None` that P5's `extract_image` requires; a match produces one observation at `zone = filename`, no span, `reliability: possible`, and **no `signal_tier`**
match_field: the filename with its final extension removed (the stem). P5 passes `file_row["filename"]`, which includes the extension; the matcher strips the last `.suffix` before applying any pattern. Patterns are anchored `^…$` against that stem.
normalization_for_matching: No normalization of the stored value. Matching applies Unicode NFC and compares case-insensitively unless a row says otherwise; the emitted value is taken from the source filename, never rebuilt.
evaluation_order: Entries are evaluated **in the order listed** and the first match wins. Order matters: `IMG_20240115_103045` must be read as the Android timestamp convention, not as an Apple/DCF sequence. Anchoring alone already separates them, and a check asserts both the anchoring and the order.
provenance_note: **v1.1 merges an independently authored version of this list.** A second version of this file (13 entries, `cfp-*` ids) was written and committed over v1.0 during the same session; it is preserved at `checks/04-alternate-version.json` and is not the live file. The two were written without sight of each other and **converged on the two decisions that matter most**: refusing the unrestricted DCF basename shape `^[A-Z0-9_]{4}[0-9]{4}$`, and flagging the `filename_pattern` return-value contract as an open question. That independent agreement is the strongest evidence available that both calls are right. v1.1 is the v1.0 superset (35 entries) plus the two rows the other version had and v1.0 lacked — its `cfp-dcf-mov` → `fnp-dcf-mov`, and its `cfp-dcf-100u` → `fnp-canon-dir-prefixed` — plus two of its refusals and two of its uncertain items. Rows it left in `uncertain` (Pixel `PXL_`, Android and Windows screenshots, Apple `IMG_E`, macOS locale forms) are live entries here, each with its own sourcing. One defect in it is recorded so it is not reintroduced — **and the first diagnosis of it, written here, was wrong.** Its `cfp-macos-screencapture` row failed this file's checker, and I recorded the cause as a capital-`S` mismatch between the pattern `^Screen ?Shot …` and the example `Screenshot …`. That was incorrect: the row sets `case_sensitive: false` and the checker applies `re.IGNORECASE`, so the pattern matches the example fine. The catalogues-finish agent traced the real cause and I reproduced it: the `example_true` was written as a bare stem with **no file extension**, and macOS puts dots in the time, so the checker's `stem()` — `rsplit('.', 1)[0]` — ate `.45 AM` as if it were an extension and matched the truncated string. The pattern was never the problem; the example was. The durable lesson, now enforced by `checks/check04.py`, is that **every example in this file must carry a file extension**, because a dotted-time convention is indistinguishable from a dotted extension without one.
design_cites: §2.6: the image record stores "filename pattern" as one of its fields, alongside format, dimensions, EXIF and software metadata.

§1.2 — the sentence that governs how this file is written: "A file called `Wash U.docx` may contain an unmistakable university application prompt; `Hw 5.pdf` may be a photographed homework page with no usable text layer; and **`IMG_4821.png` may be a screenshot of a receipt, application portal, conversation, code error, or research figure.**" The design's own example of this pattern is an example of a filename being *too weak* to conclude from.
P5 SPEC Deferred: "Camera-filename pattern library | §2.6 | That filename pattern is an emitted field; `IMG_4821.png` is the design's example | The pattern set" — this file is the missing column.
P5 SPEC E5: "E5 emits **no** photo/screenshot conclusion at all — `media type` is a Photos-domain fact (§3.11) and belongs to P6."
P5 PLAN Task 15: `emit(zone="filename", raw=matched, label=None, reliability="possible")` — the filename observation is `possible`, carries no span, and carries no tier.
rules: **A pattern names a naming convention, never a media type.** Every `pattern_label` in this file describes the convention that produced the string — "Apple/DCF camera-roll sequence", "macOS screen-capture default filename" — because that is a checkable property of the string. Whether the file *is* a photograph or a screenshot is `media type`, a Photos-domain fact, and P6's alone.

**A filename carries no `signal_tier`.** §2.6's tier table lists camera EXIF (1); capture time, GPS, sensor-shaped dimensions (2); exact display resolutions, PNG format, software metadata (3). Filenames appear in none of the three bands. This catalogue therefore cannot promote a filename into the hierarchy, and P5 emits the observation at `reliability: possible` with no tier.

**`IMG_4821` is the worked case.** It matches here as the Apple/DCF camera-roll convention. It is emphatically *not* a screenshot pattern — and it is also not proof of a camera, because iOS gives screenshots saved to Photos the same name, which is precisely §1.2's point. The row records both facts. `possible` is the design's own hedge and this file does not upgrade it.

**No date parsing.** Several conventions embed a timestamp. The patterns recognise the *shape* of the run of digits; no entry defines a date capture group, and nothing here parses, validates, normalises or emits a date. Date and academic-term extraction is §3.10's, deferred separately, and owned by P6.

**No unrestricted DCF form.** `^[A-Z0-9_]{4}[0-9]{4}$` is the standard's own generic shape and it is **refused** — it matches course codes (`MATH2010`, `ECON1001`), which is a catastrophic false positive in exactly this product's corpus. Only enumerated prefixes match. An independently written version of this list reached the same refusal.
**Absence is not evidence.** A filename matching nothing produces no observation. It is never a signal that the file is a screenshot, a photo, or anything else.
return_value_contract: Each entry carries **both** a `capture` (the regex group holding the substring of the real filename) and a `pattern_label` (the name of the convention), so the catalogue serves either reading of `filename_pattern`'s return type. Which one P5 wants is an open contract question — see `unc-return-value`, independently raised by the other version of this file as `unc-return-value-contract` — because P5 PLAN Task 15 writes `emit(zone="filename", raw=matched, …)`, making the return value the observation's `raw_value`. If `raw_value` must be source text (the safer reading of P4's RAW rules), return `capture`; if §2.6's field name "filename pattern" means the pattern itself, return `pattern_label`. Nothing else in this file changes either way.
coverage_note:
v1 covers the conventions that produce the overwhelming majority of image filenames in a personal corpus: DCF vendor prefixes (Apple, Canon, Nikon, Sony, Fujifilm, Pentax, Panasonic, Ricoh, GoPro, DJI, HTC, Samsung), the Android and Pixel timestamp conventions, the two messaging conventions that explain stripped EXIF, and the macOS / Windows / Android screen-capture defaults. It is **not** a device database: per-model quirks, Olympus month-coded names, and localized screenshot prefixes are left to `uncertain` rather than guessed.

**Two coverage limits worth stating.** First, screenshot filenames are locale-dependent — a non-English macOS writes "Bildschirmfoto", "Capture d'écran", "スクリーンショット" — and v1 covers the English defaults only. Second, iOS assigns screenshots the same `IMG_####` name as camera captures, so **there is no iOS screenshot filename pattern to write**; the absence is real, not an oversight, and §1.2 is the design acknowledging it.

sources.title: Wikipedia — Design rule for Camera File system (JEITA CP-3461)
sources.note: "The first four characters consist only of the upper-case alphanumeric characters (A - Z), (0 - 9) and the underscore `_` character, followed by a number between `0001` and `9999`, referred to as the File number. Common four-character prefixes include `DSC_`, `DSC0`, `DSCF`, `IMG_`/`MOV_`, or `P000`." Also: the `DCIM` root directory, and subdirectories of the form `100APPLE` / `101MSDCF`.

sources.title: JEITA — CP-3461 standard listing
sources.note: The standards body's own publication page for DCF.

sources.title: Canon Knowledge Base — Set the file name or file number according to the DCF standard
sources.note: Vendor confirmation of the four-character prefix plus four-digit file number scheme.

sources.title: Fairphone Community — Default camera app of Android: schema of file names
sources.note: Community sourcing (weaker than vendor docs, and the rows citing it say so) for the Android `IMG_YYYYMMDD_HHMMSS` and Samsung `YYYYMMDD_HHMMSS` conventions.

injection: `extract_image(..., filename_pattern=make_filename_pattern(load('04-camera-filename-patterns.json')))`. `filename_pattern` is a **required keyword with no default** (P5 PLAN Task 15) so that no pattern can reach `src/extractors/`. P5 PLAN's Global Constraints allow exactly one module-level regex in the whole package — `shape._LINE_BREAK_HYPHEN`, P4 D8's soft-hyphen repair — and Task 20 asserts by runtime introspection that no filename regex exists anywhere in `extractors`.

entries.rationale: The default Android camera convention. Listed before the Apple/DCF row so the intent is explicit, though the `$` anchor on that row already separates them. The optional `_1` tail is the duplicate-name suffix Android adds on collision. The digit runs are matched as shape only — no date is parsed or emitted.
Google Camera's motion photo — a still with an embedded short video. Distinct prefix, so it needs its own row rather than riding the `IMG_` one.

Android's panorama convention. Named explicitly because catalogue 03 refuses to describe panoramas by aspect ratio — the filename is the honest signal for them, and this row is what that refusal points at.
The video sibling of the Android convention. Included because §2.9 routes audio/video through the same evidence shape and a video filename is the same class of evidence.

Samsung's bare-timestamp convention. Anchored whole-stem, so it cannot fire on a digit run inside a longer name. Medium risk recorded because a bare `20240115_103045` stem could in principle come from an export script rather than a camera — but no other convention produces exactly this shape as a whole filename.

The Pixel camera convention since Android 11 — nine trailing digits, because the time carries milliseconds. Some variants append a mode suffix (`.PORTRAIT`, `.MP`), captured by the optional group but excluded from the capture.

iOS writes the edited version of a photo as `IMG_E1234` beside the original `IMG_1234`. Listed before the plain Apple row because `E` would otherwise be read as part of a sequence number. Also a genuine version-family signal (G5), though establishing that is P6's.

**The design's own example, and the acceptance case for this file.** `IMG_` is one of the four-character prefixes JEITA CP-3461 names, followed by the DCF file number. Canon uses the same prefix. It is catalogued as a *camera file system naming convention* — a checkable property of the string — and **not** as a media-type verdict. Two things are true at once and both are recorded: this is the camera-roll convention, and §1.2 says `IMG_4821.png` "may be a screenshot of a receipt, application portal, conversation, code error, or research figure", because iOS gives screenshots saved to Photos the same name. That ambiguity is exactly why P5 emits this at `reliability: possible` with no `signal_tier`, and why nothing downstream may treat it as proof of either reading. The five-digit alternative covers rolls that have passed 9999.
entries.design_cite: §1.2 "`IMG_4821.png` may be a screenshot of a receipt, application portal, conversation, code error, or research figure"; P5 SPEC Deferred "`IMG_4821.png` is the design's example"
entries.source: JEITA CP-3461 via Wikipedia; Canon KB ART156893

entries.rationale: The video sibling of `IMG_`, named in the same JEITA sentence — the standard lists the common prefixes as "`DSC_`, `DSC0`, `DSCF`, `IMG_`/`MOV_`, or `P000`". **Merged in from the independently authored version of this list (`cfp-dcf-mov`), which had it where v1.0 did not.**

Older Canon EOS bodies name files with the DCIM directory number and the file number — `100_0001.JPG` in `100CANON`. **Merged in from the independently authored version (`cfp-dcf-100u`)**, generalised from its literal `100_` to `1NN_` because the directory number increments to `101`, `102` and beyond. Medium risk: the shape is all digits and an underscore, so a document named `100_2024` would match; anchoring to the whole stem and requiring a leading `1` is what keeps it narrow.
entries.source: JEITA CP-3461 via Wikipedia (`100APPLE`/`101MSDCF` directory form)

entries.rationale: Canon writes a leading underscore in place of the first prefix character when the colour space is Adobe RGB — the DCF convention for signalling non-sRGB. Case-sensitive because the underscore-prefix form is defined on uppercase.
The older Canon RAW naming, with its Adobe RGB underscore variant.
`DSC_` is named in the DCF standard's own list of common prefixes. Nikon's Adobe RGB variant moves the underscore to the front.
Nikon's Adobe RGB form, distinct from `DSC_####` by underscore position.
The Coolpix compact line's prefix.
Sony uses `DSC0` as its four-character prefix — the standard's `DSC0` entry — which reads as `DSC` plus five digits. Distinguished from the Nikon row by the absence of the underscore.
`DSCF` is named in the DCF standard's own prefix list; Fujifilm is its main user.
Pentax's four-character prefix. Anchored, so it cannot be confused with `IMG_####`.

`P000` is named in the DCF standard's prefix list; Panasonic and Olympus both produce a `P` followed by seven digits. Exactly eight characters, matching the DCF basename length, which is what makes the anchored pattern safe. Subsumes the narrower `^P000\d{4}$` the other version of this list used.
Ricoh's eight-character DCF basename.
HTC's prefix, corroborated by the Android Central thread.
The prefix used by Samsung's compact and bridge cameras, distinct from the Galaxy phone timestamp convention.
GoPro's original naming for a single photo or the first chapter of a video.
GoPro's chaptered naming: two letters identifying the encoding, then a two-digit chapter and a four-digit file number.
DJI drone and gimbal camera naming.
The newer DJI convention on Mini and Air models. Shape only; the fourteen-digit run is not parsed.
A widely used older prefix across Minolta, Casio and Kodak compacts. Common in an archive of pre-2010 photos.

**This row exists because of §2.6's first trap.** §2.6 warns that "messaging platforms and downloaded web images often strip metadata from real photographs", and P5 is forbidden from writing an absence. A WhatsApp filename is the *positive* evidence that explains the missing EXIF — a reading of a value that is present, not an inference from one that is not. It says the file arrived through WhatsApp; it says nothing about whether the content is a photograph, and P6 decides that. Note the hyphens: WhatsApp uses `IMG-`, not the DCF `IMG_`, so this cannot collide with the Apple row. Independently present in the other version of this list.
entries.design_cite: §2.6 "Messaging platforms and downloaded web images often strip metadata from real photographs"

entries.rationale: The video sibling of the WhatsApp row, same reasoning.
Signal's export naming. Same role as the WhatsApp rows: positive evidence of a messaging origin, which is what §2.6 wants in place of reasoning from stripped metadata.

entries.pattern_label: macOS screen-capture default filename (Ventura and later)
entries.rationale: macOS's default screenshot name. The optional AM/PM segment is locale- and clock-setting dependent, and the space before it is a narrow no-break space (U+202F) on recent macOS — a real trap, since a plain space will not match. English locale only; see the coverage note. Note the defect avoided here: the other version of this list wrote `^Screen ?Shot …` with a capital `S` on `Shot`, which cannot match modern macOS's one-word `Screenshot`; the two spellings are two rows in this file.

entries.pattern_label: macOS screen-capture default filename (pre-Ventura, two words)
entries.rationale: macOS wrote "Screen Shot" as two words before Ventura. Both forms are common in an archive spanning several years.
The video sibling of the macOS screenshot convention.
The name Windows gives captures saved by Win+PrtScn into Pictures\Screenshots. Anchored on the parenthesised counter, so prose cannot match.
The Windows 11 Snipping Tool's date-and-time form, distinguished from the macOS row by having no " at " separator and no dots in the time.

Android's convention, with both the hyphen and underscore separators that different vendors use. The optional trailing group absorbs the app name some builds append (`Screenshot_20240115-103045_Chrome`), which is deliberately **not** captured — an app name is a value P6 might rank, and inventing it here would be P5 deciding meaning.

CleanShot X's default naming, including its `@2x` Retina suffix. Pairs with catalogue 01's `tps-cleanshot`, which catches the same tool when it stamps image `Software` metadata — two independent readings of the same origin.

refused.rationale: **The most important refusal in this file, and the one an independently written version of this list also reached** (its `ref-generic-dcf-basename`). This is JEITA CP-3461's own generic form — four uppercase alphanumerics or underscores, then four digits — and it is exactly the shape of a course code. `MATH2010`, `ECON1001`, `CHEM1220` and `PHYS2020` all match it — and so, as the catalogues-finish agent pointed out independently, do **`FALL2024`** and **`NOTE2024`**. `FALL2024` is the sharpest case on the page: it is an academic term name, which §3.10 owns, so the unrestricted pattern would not merely mislabel a file, it would reach across a part boundary and manufacture a camera reading out of a date, and a screenshot of a course page saved as `MATH2010.png` would be read as a camera file. This product's central worked example is a course code (`BUSIB 4300`, §3.2), so the false positive is not hypothetical — it is aimed at the corpus the product exists to organize. Only the enumerated vendor prefixes match. A safer gated variant is proposed in `unc-dcf-generic-in-dcim`.
refused.design_cite: §3.2 `subject = BUSIB 4300`; §3.10 "file names and documents frequently contain numbers that look like years but are course identifiers"

refused.rationale: A prefix match on the word would catch `Screenshot of the enrollment error.png` — a file a person deliberately named, whose name is real evidence about content that P6 should read as text, not as a convention marker. Only the dated machine-generated forms match. The distinction this file draws is between a name a *tool* generated and a name a *person* wrote. Independently reached by the other version as `ref-screenshot-word-anywhere`.
Would match `IMGs for the poster`, `IMG_final_v3`, and every hand-edited derivative. The digit-run anchor is what makes the Apple row a convention match rather than a prefix guess.

Some cameras and export tools drop the prefix and leave `0142.JPG`. Matching it would claim every four-digit filename in the corpus — years, invoice numbers, page scans, exported slides. **Merged in from the other version of this list (`ref-bare-sequence-number`)**, which had this refusal where v1.0 did not state it. Nothing distinguishes a bare number from a bare number.
refused.design_cite: §2.6 "filename pattern"; §3.10 "numbers that look like years but are course identifiers, version numbers, build numbers, ZIP codes"

refused.rationale: **There is none, and the absence is the finding.** iOS saves screenshots into Photos under the same `IMG_####` camera-roll sequence as captures, so no filename distinguishes them. This is not a gap to be filled later; writing one would mean inventing a distinction the platform does not make. It is also the concrete reason §1.2 uses `IMG_4821.png` as its example of a filename that cannot be relied on.
refused.design_cite: §1.2 "`IMG_4821.png` may be a screenshot of a receipt, application portal, conversation, code error, or research figure"
refused.cross_match_expected: `IMG_4821` is expected to match `fnp-apple-dcf-img`. That is the whole point of this row: because iOS makes no distinct screenshot filename, an iOS screenshot falls through to the camera-roll convention and is read as `possible`, tier-less evidence of that convention and nothing more.

uncertain.rationale: **A contract question for the P5 owner, not a data question — and raised independently by both versions of this file, which is the strongest signal available that it genuinely needs answering.** P5 PLAN Task 15 does `emit(zone="filename", raw=matched, label=None, reliability="possible")`, so whatever `filename_pattern` returns becomes the observation's `raw_value`. Returning the matched substring (`IMG_4821`) keeps `raw_value` as source text, consistent with P4's RAW discipline. Returning the convention name (`Apple/DCF camera-roll sequence`) matches §2.6's field name "filename pattern" but puts a P5-authored label in a raw slot. Every entry carries both, so the answer changes no data here — but it should be settled before E5 is implemented.
uncertain.design_cite: P4 RAW-1/RAW-2; §2.6 "filename pattern"; P5 PLAN Task 15

uncertain.pattern: ^[A-Z0-9_]{4}[0-9]{4}$ gated on a DCIM ancestor directory
uncertain.rationale: The safe form of the refused generic pattern: apply it only when an ancestor directory is `DCIM` or matches `^\d{3}[A-Z0-9]{5}$` (`100APPLE`, `101MSDCF`), both defined by the DCF standard. A course code will not sit under `DCIM`. Not adopted in v1 because `filename_pattern(filename)` receives only the filename — the path is not in scope — so adopting it means widening P5's injected signature, which is the P5 owner's decision and not one to take from a catalogue.
uncertain.design_cite: JEITA CP-3461 DCIM root and `100APPLE`-form subdirectories; P4 zone `path` for parent-folder context

uncertain.rationale: Copies and burst frames append suffixes that break the anchored patterns: `IMG_4821 (1).png`, `IMG_4821-2.jpg`, `IMG_20240115_103045_BURST001_COVER.jpg`. The Android rows already absorb a `_N` tail and the Pixel row absorbs a mode suffix, but the general case is unhandled, so a duplicated photo silently matches nothing. **Raised by the other version of this list (`unc-duplicate-and-burst-suffixes`) and adopted here.** Worth fixing, and the fix interacts with G5's version-family signals — a `(1)` suffix is exactly the "a filename suffix alone is never enough" case P6 SPEC refuses to treat as a version signal on its own, so the two decisions should be made together.
uncertain.design_cite: §2.9 "duplicate and version-family signals"; P6 SPEC G5
uncertain.cross_match_expected: `IMG_4821.png` is expected to match `fnp-apple-dcf-img` — that is the contrast this row is making. The unsuffixed name matches; the suffixed `IMG_4821 (1).png` matches nothing, which is the gap being reported.

uncertain.pattern: Bildschirmfoto / Capture d'écran / Captura de pantalla / スクリーンショット / 屏幕快照
uncertain.rationale: macOS and Android localize the screenshot filename prefix. v1 covers English only. Worth adding if Joseph's corpus is not English-locale — a single question that would settle it. Guessing the exact localized date formats without a real file to check would be inventing. Independently flagged by the other version as `unc-macos-locale-forms`.

Olympus encodes the month as a single character (1-9 then A, B, C for October to December) and the day as two digits. The shape collides with the plain `P#######` Panasonic row for months 1-9, so `fnp-panasonic-p` already catches most of them; only October-December names differ. Not separated in v1 because the distinction buys nothing — both readings say "a DCF camera wrote this".
uncertain.cross_match_expected: `P1010042` is expected to match `fnp-panasonic-p`. Olympus names for January-September are the same shape as Panasonic's, so the existing row already catches them; only October-December (`PA`, `PB`, `PC`) differ, and both readings say the same thing — a DCF camera wrote this.

uncertain.rationale: Telegram (`photo_1234@15-01-2024_10-30-45`) and Instagram saved-post naming would extend the messaging class, which is the class that explains stripped EXIF under §2.6's trap 1. Both are community-reported with format variation across versions and platforms, so they are recorded rather than guessed. One real exported file each would settle them.
uncertain.design_cite: §2.6 "Messaging platforms and downloaded web images often strip metadata from real photographs"

uncertain.rationale: Flatbed and multifunction scanners write their own conventions (`Scan_20240115`, `Scanned Document`, `Image (3)`). A scanner class would pair with catalogue 01's `unc-scanner-mfp` row. Left out of v1 because the naming is per-vendor and per-driver, and `Image (3)` in particular is far too generic to match safely.

uncertain.pattern: further Canon prefixes (`_MG_`, `CRW_`, `1NN_`) and their overlap
uncertain.rationale: Canon has used at least four naming schemes across its EOS, PowerShot and legacy lines. Three are live entries here; the other version of this list left the whole family in `uncertain` (its `unc-canon-prefixes`), which is a defensible alternative reading. The residual risk sits on `fnp-canon-dir-prefixed`, whose `1NN_####` shape is the least distinctive pattern in the file. If it proves noisy, drop that row first.

sourcing_note: **How to read the `verification` column, because it is not decoration.** Only five pages were opened and read directly while authoring these catalogues; three more were opened by the catalogues-finish agent, who supplied verbatim quotes. Everything else is marked `search_summary`: the fact came from a web-search result summary and the page itself was not retrieved. Those rows say `consulted` rather than `retrieved`, because claiming a retrieval date for a page nobody opened is exactly the kind of unearned confidence these catalogues exist to keep out of the product. A `search_summary` source is not worthless — it is how most of the vendor-prefix and manifest-name knowledge here was gathered — but it must not be quoted as if read, and a row that would be harmful if wrong should be upgraded before launch.
example_semantics: **`example_false` means something different here than in catalogue 01, and the difference is deliberate.** In catalogue 01 an `example_false` must match *no row in the file* — it proves a string is not a tool name at all. In this file the rows are sibling conventions that share prefixes, so an `example_false` proves *this row does not claim a string that a different row rightly claims*: `IMG_20240115_103045.jpg` must not read as an Apple/DCF sequence, and it must read as the Android timestamp convention. Where that is the intent the row names the winner in `discriminates_from`, and `checks/check04.py` asserts the collision lands on exactly that row — so a *new* collision, or one that moves to the wrong row, still fails. Leaving the intent implicit is how a wrong diagnosis hid once already; see `provenance_note`.
